Customising plots

Source: vignettes/articles/custom-plotting.Rmd
custom-plotting.Rmd

Apply a theme to every panel

{gratia}’s draw() combines the individual plots for model terms into one figure using {patchwork}. The & operator applies a {ggplot2} theme to every panel, so you can style them together.

Load the plotting packages and simulate 400 observations. The covariates are independent and range from zero to one. Three have nonlinear effects on the mean response; x3 has no true effect. Independent Gaussian noise adds variation with standard deviation 2.

library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("ggplot2")
library("dplyr")
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library("patchwork")

# simulate data
n <- 400
eg1 <- data_sim("eg1", n = n, seed = 1)

Fit a Gaussian GAM with one smooth for each covariate. REML selects the smoothness; we will reuse this fitted model throughout the plotting examples.

# fit model
m <- gam(y ~ s(x0) + s(x1) + s(x2) + s(x3),
  data = eg1, method = "REML")

Save the default figure as p so we can apply different styles to the same fitted smooths.

p <- draw(m)
p

Adding a theme with + changes only the last panel in this combined figure. The following example makes that behaviour visible: only the final smooth receives the white background from theme_bw().

p + theme_bw()

Use & to apply the same theme to all four panels.

p & theme_bw()

Change curve colours, intervals and other plot components

gratia has theme settings for smooth curves, interval ribbons, residual points and reference lines. Here we make every smooth navy, give it a thicker line and use a pale navy interval ribbon.

p & theme(
  geom.gratia.smooth = element_geom(colour = "navy", linewidth = 0.8),
  geom.gratia.interval = element_geom(fill = "navy"),
  gratia.alpha.interval = 0.15
)

Use geom.gratia.partial.residual for partial residuals, geom.gratia.diagnostic.point for diagnostic points, and geom.gratia.reference for reference lines. Opacity uses numeric settings such as gratia.alpha.interval and gratia.alpha.diagnostic.point. More specific settings, such as geom.gratia.smooth.interval, override the general interval setting. See ?gratia_theme_get for the component list.

Use gratia_theme_set() when you want subsequent gratia figures to share a style. Save its return value so you can restore the previous settings after drawing the figure.

old_theme <- gratia_theme_set(theme(gratia.alpha.interval = 0.1))
draw(m)

gratia_theme_set(old_theme)

These settings affect gratia plots created afterwards. For a temporary change, you can instead use withr::with_options() with the gratia.plot.theme option. If you have older code using arguments such as smooth_col or ci_alpha, replace those arguments with theme settings as shown above.

Common replacements for deprecated arguments are:

Previous argument Theme setting
smooth_col geom.gratia.smooth = element_geom(colour = ...)
ci_col, ci_alpha geom.gratia.interval = element_geom(fill = ...), gratia.alpha.interval
resid_col geom.gratia.partial.residual = element_geom(colour = ...)
contour_col geom.gratia.contour = element_geom(colour = ...)
point_col, point_alpha in diagnostics geom.gratia.diagnostic.point = element_geom(colour = ...), gratia.alpha.diagnostic.point
line_col in diagnostics geom.gratia.diagnostic.reference = element_geom(colour = ...)
colour, alpha in smooth samples geom.gratia.sample = element_geom(colour = ...), gratia.alpha.sample
ci_3d_col, ci_3d_alpha geom.gratia.surface.interval = element_geom(fill = ...), gratia.alpha.surface.interval
alpha, linewidth in chain diagnostics gratia.alpha.chain, geom.gratia.chain = element_geom(linewidth = ...)

Use geom.gratia.effect for parametric curves and geom.gratia.derivative for derivatives. Rootograms have separate rootogram.bar, rootogram.fitted, rootogram.reference and rootogram.warning elements. MRF interval lines use geom.gratia.smooth.interval, independently of the points controlled by geom.gratia.smooth. Diagnostic boxplots use geom.gratia.diagnostic.boxplot.

Laying out labels, legends and colour bars

Long labels can overlap when several plots share a figure. Use draw_label_control() to choose wrapping widths and guide layouts, then pass the result as label_control to draw() or assemble(). The configuration works across drawing methods.

For a categorical axis, wrapping breaks long labels into lines and n_dodge staggers labels across rows. We simulate observations in three fishing categories so we can illustrate both options. The response combines a curved effect of day, a difference between categories and independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.3.

set.seed(430)
fishing <- data.frame(
  day = runif(150, 0, 300),
  angler_type = factor(rep(c("Boat (guided)", "Boat (unguided)", "Shore"), 50))
)
fishing$y <- sin(fishing$day / 60) +
  c(0, -0.8, -0.3)[as.integer(fishing$angler_type)] + rnorm(150, sd = 0.3)

Fit a GAM with a smooth effect of day and a parametric effect of fishing category. Wrap the fishing-category labels and stagger them over two rows.

fishing_model <- gam(y ~ angler_type + s(day, k = 8),
  data = fishing, method = "REML")
axis_layout <- draw_label_control(axes = list(wrap = 12, n_dodge = 2))
draw(fishing_model, label_control = axis_layout, ncol = 2)

Legends have their own wrapping width and can arrange their entries into rows or columns. Compare the fitted day smooth with one that has a smaller basis and no smoothing penalty (fx = TRUE). The smaller basis limits how much the curve can bend. Use descriptive labels for the two fits and wrap the entries in a single legend column.

simple_fishing <- gam(y ~ angler_type + s(day, k = 3, fx = TRUE),
  data = fishing, method = "REML")
comparison <- compare_smooths(fishing_model, simple_fishing, n = 50)
comparison$.model <- factor(comparison$.model,
  levels = c("fishing_model", "simple_fishing"),
  labels = c("More flexible curve across the season", "Less flexible curve across the season"))
legend_layout <- draw_label_control(
  legend = list(wrap = 22, title_wrap = 18, ncol = 1)
)
draw(comparison, label_control = legend_layout)

Colour bars can wrap their titles, rotate their tick labels, and change their displayed dimensions. The following pairwise concurvity plot shows how closely each smooth can be approximated by another smooth in the four-smooth model. The fill scale supplies the title and the label control wraps it and sets the bar height. Use the scale to set the palette, breaks and numeric labels.

bar_layout <- draw_label_control(
  axes = list(wrap = 15),
  colourbar = list(title_wrap = 18, height = grid::unit(35, "mm"))
)
draw(model_concurvity(m, pairwise = TRUE),
  continuous_colour = scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Concurvity between model terms"),
  label_control = bar_layout)

Wrapping happens after scale labels have been formatted, preserving custom labels, mathematical expressions and explicit line breaks. Use axes = list(title_wrap = ...) to wrap axis titles. Wrapping and staggering tick labels applies only to discrete axes.

Use a different palette for groups

Grouped curves and ribbons use the Okabe–Ito palette for up to nine groups, and a hue palette for more than nine. Supply a palette function to both the colour and fill theme settings to keep each model’s curve and interval the same colour. Here we use Paul Tol’s bright palette for the model comparison.

tol <- gratia_palette("tol_bright")
draw(comparison) &
  theme(palette.colour.discrete = tol, palette.fill.discrete = tol)

Paul Tol choices include bright and vibrant (7 colours), muted (9), dark (11), and banded schemes (12, 16 or 20). The dark palette is designed for a white background. Choose a palette with enough colours for all your groups. A request for more colours than the palette provides gives an error. See ?gratia_palette for available names.

Continuous palettes can also be changed through palette.fill.continuous and palette.colour.continuous. Existing scale arguments still accept complete scales when custom transformations, breaks or guides are needed.

Combining individual plots produced by draw()

Each draw() result is already a combined figure, even if it contains only one smooth. When combining several results, specify their layout explicitly. First, here is the error that can occur when those dimensions are omitted.

p1 <- draw(m, select = "s(x0)")
p2 <- draw(m, select = "s(x1)")
p3 <- draw(m, select = "s(x2)")
p1 + p2 + p3
#> Error in `wrap_dims()`:
#> ! Need 3 panels, but together `nrow` and `ncol` only provide 1.
#> ℹ Please increase `ncol` and/or `nrow`.

Add plot_layout(ncol = 3) to place the three results in one row.

p1 + p2 + p3 + plot_layout(ncol = 3)

When all smooths come from the same model, select them in one draw() call and supply ncol directly.

draw(m, select = c("s(x0)", "s(x1)", "s(x2)"), ncol = 3)

The explicit layout is useful when the plots come from different models or need to be arranged with other ggplot2 figures.

Grouping factor smooths and showing their intervals

grouped selects which factor smooth types share a plot. Choose any of "factor-by", "sz", and "fs". Types omitted from the vector are drawn separately for each level, or each evaluated combination of levels for sz terms with several factors. show_ci independently selects which of these types show interval ribbons. These controls apply to curves with one continuous covariate; ordinary smooths and surface plots retain their displays.

The defaults, grouped = c("sz", "fs") and show_ci = c("factor-by", "sz"), retain the existing grouping and interval visibility. Use FALSE to select none. Separate curves use the usual univariate styling: a black fitted line and a translucent black interval. We simulate x2 between zero and one and use fac to identify three groups. The response combines a different curve of x2 in each group with independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation 2. We then fit three ways of representing these relationships. A factor-by smooth fits a curve for each group; an sz smooth represents group deviations from a shared curve; an fs smooth estimates group curves whose penalties share smoothing parameters.

factor_data <- data_sim("eg4", n = 400, seed = 244)

Fit the three representations to the same data so we can compare how their group curves are displayed. Each model uses REML to select its smoothing parameters.

m_by <- gam(y ~ fac + s(x2, by = fac), data = factor_data, method = "REML")
m_sz <- gam(y ~ s(x2) + s(x2, fac, bs = "sz"),
  data = factor_data, method = "REML")
m_fs <- gam(y ~ s(x2, fac, bs = "fs"),
  data = factor_data, method = "REML")

Overlay the factor-by curves with intervals:

draw(m_by, grouped = "factor-by", parametric = FALSE)

Separate the sz deviations and hide their intervals. The ordinary smooth retains its interval:

draw(m_sz, grouped = FALSE, show_ci = "factor-by")

fs terms represent a fitted curve for each factor level. Separate those curves and include their intervals with:

draw(m_fs, grouped = FALSE, show_ci = "fs")

The same controls work with saved estimates. Grouping the curves or hiding their intervals leaves the saved estimates and interval limits intact. Here we draw each group deviation separately and omit its interval ribbon.

sz_estimates <- smooth_estimates(m_sz)
draw(sz_estimates, grouped = FALSE, show_ci = FALSE)

Ordered-factor by smooths use "factor-by" too. In the following model, s(x2) is the reference smooth and the ordered-factor terms describe deviations for the other levels. Grouping overlays only those deviations; the reference smooth remains a separate plot. No smooth is created for the ordered factor’s first level, and the displayed deviations do not have the reference smooth added to them.

factor_data$ordered_fac <- ordered(factor_data$fac)
m_ordered <- gam(y ~ fac + s(x2) + s(x2, by = ordered_fac),
  data = factor_data, method = "REML")
draw(m_ordered, grouped = "factor-by", parametric = FALSE)

grouped_by is deprecated. Replace grouped_by = TRUE with grouped = c("factor-by", "sz", "fs"); replace grouped_by = FALSE with grouped = c("sz", "fs"). During migration, an explicit grouped_by updates only "factor-by" membership in grouped.

Drawing surfaces in 3D

With the optional {ggcube} package installed, use surface = "3d" to view a two-dimensional smooth as a surface. First simulate a nonlinear response over two covariates with independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.2, so the surface’s peaks remain visible above the noise.

eg2 <- data_sim("eg2", n = 400, scale = 0.2, seed = 2)

Fit a tensor product smooth with 15 basis functions per covariate to allow enough flexibility for the nonlinear surface; REML selects its smoothness. Then draw the smooth’s contribution to the linear predictor. n_2d = 50 evaluates the surface on a 50-by-50 grid, and yaw controls the viewing angle.

m_surface <- gam(y ~ te(x, z, k = c(15, 15)),
  data = eg2, method = "REML")
draw(m_surface, surface = "3d", n_2d = 50,
  surface_3d = list(yaw = 45, persp = FALSE))

Pass camera settings through surface_3d, which forwards them to ggcube::coord_3d(). For example, persp = FALSE uses a parallel projection so distant parts of the surface do not appear smaller.

The covariates form the two horizontal axes and the partial effect forms the vertical axis. Use surface = "tile" for a flat rectangular display or the default surface = "raster" for a compact image. These choices display the same estimated effect.

Build a plot from smooth estimates and partial residuals

Themes control the appearance of plots returned by draw(). To choose different layers or map additional variables to aesthetics, build a plot from the estimates returned by gratia.

First evaluate the fitted smooths with smooth_estimates() and add pointwise interval limits with add_confint(). Each row contains a value of the covariate, the estimated smooth at that value and its interval limits.

# evaluate the smooths
sm <- smooth_estimates(m) |>
  add_confint()
sm
#> # A tibble: 400 × 11
#>    .smooth .type .by   .estimate   .se     x0    x1    x2    x3 .lower_ci
#>    <chr>   <chr> <chr>     <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1 s(x0)   TPRS  NA       -0.929 0.422 0.0131    NA    NA    NA    -1.76 
#>  2 s(x0)   TPRS  NA       -0.881 0.396 0.0230    NA    NA    NA    -1.66 
#>  3 s(x0)   TPRS  NA       -0.834 0.372 0.0329    NA    NA    NA    -1.56 
#>  4 s(x0)   TPRS  NA       -0.786 0.348 0.0429    NA    NA    NA    -1.47 
#>  5 s(x0)   TPRS  NA       -0.738 0.326 0.0528    NA    NA    NA    -1.38 
#>  6 s(x0)   TPRS  NA       -0.690 0.305 0.0627    NA    NA    NA    -1.29 
#>  7 s(x0)   TPRS  NA       -0.643 0.287 0.0727    NA    NA    NA    -1.20 
#>  8 s(x0)   TPRS  NA       -0.595 0.270 0.0826    NA    NA    NA    -1.12 
#>  9 s(x0)   TPRS  NA       -0.548 0.255 0.0925    NA    NA    NA    -1.05 
#> 10 s(x0)   TPRS  NA       -0.501 0.242 0.102     NA    NA    NA    -0.975
#> # ℹ 390 more rows
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: .upper_ci <dbl>

To add partial residual points, use add_partial_residuals() on the fitting data. In this Gaussian model with an identity link, a partial residual for a smooth is the observation minus the fitted intercept and the contributions of the other terms. These are the points shown by draw(m, residuals = TRUE).

# add partial residuals to data
eg1 <- eg1 |>
  add_partial_residuals(m)

The new columns use the smooth labels as names, such as s(x0) and s(x1). Inspect the names so we can select the column matching the smooth to plot.

names(eg1)
#>  [1] "y"     "x0"    "x1"    "x2"    "x3"    "f"     "f0"    "f1"    "f2"   
#> [10] "f3"    "s(x0)" "s(x1)" "s(x2)" "s(x3)"

Plot the smooth for x2 using five layers:

  1. a rug plot of the observed values of x2,
  2. the credible interval around the estimated smooth,
  3. the partial residuals as a point layer,
  4. the estimated smooth as a line layer,
  5. an axis label and title.
p_sx2 <- sm |>
  filter(.smooth == "s(x2)") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x2),
    data = eg1,
    sides = "b", length = grid::unit(0.02, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, x = x2),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = x2, y = `s(x2)`),
    data = eg1, size = 1.5, colour = "steelblue3"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x2, y = .estimate), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Partial effect", title = "s(x2)")
p_sx2

We prepare equivalent plots for the other three smooths to combine with this one below. Their construction repeats the same steps, so the code is hidden.

Combine the four plots and set ncol = 2 to arrange them in two columns.

p_sx0 + p_sx1 + p_sx2 + p_sx3 + plot_layout(ncol = 2)

Colour partial residuals by another variable

A custom plot can show information beyond the variables in the fitted smooth. To demonstrate grouping, create an arbitrary four-level factor and use it to colour the residual points. This factor is unrelated to the simulated response and is used only to demonstrate the colour mapping.

set.seed(12)
eg1 <- eg1 |>
  mutate(fac = sample(letters[1:4], n(), replace = TRUE))

Build the curve and interval first, then add the partial residuals with fac mapped to colour. Adding the points last keeps them visible above the interval ribbon.

plt <- sm |>
  filter(.smooth == "s(x2)") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x2),
    data = eg1,
    sides = "b", length = grid::unit(0.02, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, x = x2),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x2, y = .estimate), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Partial effect", title = "s(x2)")

plt +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      x = x2, y = `s(x2)`,
      colour = fac
    ),
    data = eg1, size = 1.5
  )

To look for patterns involving another fitted covariate, map x1 to point colour and size. We remove the fixed point size so it can vary with x1.

plt +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      x = x2, y = `s(x2)`,
      colour = x1, size = x1
    ),
    data = eg1, alpha = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "plasma")

If points of the same colour consistently fall above or below the fitted curve, residuals may still vary with x1. The model diagnostics article shows how to check that pattern by plotting residuals directly against a covariate.
